newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal government faces key test in by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Nepal government faces key test in by-elections.

text.p: Nepali Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba, who heads a fragile coalition government, faces a critical test in five parliamentary by-elections this week, analysts said on Wednesday.
"It (the by-elections) will be a strong indicator of public opinion," said Ganesh Raj Sharma, a well-known constitutional lawyer and analyst.

About 320,000 voters in the Himalayan kingdom on Friday pick from among 46 candidates to fill five vacant seats in the lower house of parliament in the first ballot since Deuba's fractious coalition took power 17 months ago.
Campaigning for the by-elections ended at midnight on Tuesday. The results are expected to be announced by Sunday.
Politicians see the by-election as a litmus test for Deuba, criticised for a lacklustre performance and a failure to check corruption in Nepal, one of the world's 10 poorest countries.

The coalition led by the centrist Nepali Congress party narrowly survived a no-confidence motion last December, when the communist-led opposition fell two votes short of the 103 needed to topple the government in the 205-seat parliament.

Deuba had only 84 votes from his own party in the no-confidence vote, raising doubts about his ability to prove his majority. It prompted the main opposition United Marxist Leninist (UML) party to seek his resignation.

Deuba remains in power since he was not legally required to resign but his authority has been challenged by rivals. He has vowed to seek a confidence vote in the next session of parliament scheduled to begin late in February.

On paper, Deuba's coalition commands a 108-member majority with his Nepali Congress controlling 86 deputies, and its partners, the Rastriya Prajatantra Party (RPP) 19 seats and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP) three.
But the partners are sharply divided.
The UML controls 87 seats and the remaining five seats are shared by independents and a small leftist party.
Deuba's main problem stemmed from a split in the RPP.
As part of moves to shore up his support, Deuba has re-appointed five former rebel RPP ministers who resigned to vote against him in December, but attracted criticism from his own party.
If the Nepali Congress wins a majority of the seats in Friday's polls, the country would be on its way to political stability, party general secretary Taranath Rana Bhatt said.
"This will strengthen Deuba's position in bargaining with coalition partners," Bhatt told Reuters.
But UML's general decretary Madhav Kumar Nepal said his party was better placed to win seats and force Deuba out.
